596970.title: Boscastle
596970.extract:
Boscastle (Cornish: Kastelboterel) is a village and fishing port on the north coast of Cornwall, England, in the civil parish of Forrabury and Minster (where the 2011 Census population was included) . It is 14 miles (23 km) south of Bude and 5 miles (8 km) northeast of Tintagel. The harbour is a natural inlet protected by two stone harbour walls built in 1584 by Sir Richard Grenville and is the only significant harbour for 20 miles (32 km) along the coast. The village extends up the valleys of the River Valency and River Jordan. Heavy rainfall on 16 August 2004 caused extensive damage to the village.
Boscastle lies within the Cornwall National Landscape (formerly Cornwall Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, or AONB). The South West Coast Path passes through the village.

'''Boscastle''' ({{langx|kw|Kastelboterel}})<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.magakernow.org.uk/default.aspx?page=520 |title=Cornish Language Partnership : Place names in the SWF |publisher=Magakernow.org.uk |access-date=9 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515091028/http://www.magakernow.org.uk/default.aspx?page=520 |archive-date=15 May 2013 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref> is a village and [[fishing]] [[port]] on the north coast of [[Cornwall]], England, in the [[civil parishes in England|civil parish]] of [[Forrabury and Minster]] (where the 2011 Census population was included) . It is {{convert|14|mi|km}} south of [[Bude]] and {{convert|5|mi|km|0}} northeast of [[Tintagel]].<ref>Ordnance Survey: Landranger map sheet 190 ''Bude & Clovelly'' {{ISBN|978-0-319-23145-6}}</ref> The [[harbour]] is a natural inlet protected by two stone harbour walls built in 1584 by Sir [[Richard Grenville]] and is the only significant harbour for {{convert|20|mi|km}} along the coast. The village extends up the valleys of the [[River Valency]] and [[River Jordan, Cornwall|River Jordan]]. Heavy rainfall on 16 August 2004 caused extensive damage to the village.

Boscastle lies within the [[Cornwall National Landscape]] (formerly Cornwall Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, or AONB). The [[South West Coast Path]] passes through the village.

==History==
Boscastle was first inhabited by the Bottreaux family around 1080,<ref name=Bottreaux /> and the name of the village comes from [[Bottreaux Castle]] (pronounced "Botro"),<ref>As is pronounced the name of the former Devon manor of [[Molland|Molland-Bottreaux]], a remnant of which name survives as the hamlet of Bottreaux Mill, Molland; also the title [[Baron Botreaux]]. Pointon, Graham E. (1990). ''BBC Pronouncing Dictionary of British Names'' (2nd ed.) Oxford: Oxford University Press; p. 31</ref> a 12th-century [[motte-and-bailey]] fortress, of which few remains survive. The castle, built sometime between 1154 and 1189 by Sir William des Bottreaux,<ref name=Bottreaux>{{cite web|title=Bottreaux Castle|url=https://www.waymarking.com/waymarks/WMP7HP_Bottreaux_Castle_Boscastle_Cornwall|publisher=Waymaking|access-date=18 October 2021}}</ref> was anciently in the possession of the de Botreaux family, which became under [[William de Botreaux, 1st Baron Botreaux|William de Botreaux]] (1337–91) the [[Baron Botreaux|Barons Botreaux]]. It was to the father of William 1st Baron Botreaux, also William, that [[Edward II]] granted a charter in 1312 to hold a market at Boscastle, along with a fair on the [[Feast of Saint James]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://archives.history.ac.uk/gazetteer/cornwall.html |title= CORNWALL |date= 17 November 2006 |website= GAZETTEER OF MARKETS AND FAIRS IN ENGLAND AND WALES TO 1516 |publisher= Centre for Metropolitan History |access-date= 5 December 2021}}</ref>

The [[antiquary]], [[John Leland (antiquary)|John Leland]] in the mid 16th century described the village ″''... it is a very filthy town and il kept.''″<ref>{{cite news|title=On the North Coast (Continued from our last)|work=The Cornishman|issue=17|date=14 November 1878|page=4}}</ref> Boscastle [[harbour]] is a natural inlet protected by two stone harbour walls built in 1584 by Sir [[Richard Grenville]] (of [[English ship Revenge (1577)|''Revenge'']]). It is the only significant harbour for {{convert|20|mi|km}} along the coast. Boscastle was once a small port (similar to many others on the north coast of Cornwall), importing limestone and coal, and exporting slate and other local produce.
By 1848 the population was 807.<ref>{{cite book |title=The National Cyclopaedia of Useful Knowledge |date=1848 |publisher=Charles Knight |location=London |page=Vol. IV, p. 965 |edition=First}}</ref>

In the early 20th century Boscastle hosted a street dance similar to the [[Helston]] [[Furry Dance]],<ref>{{cite book |last = Hambly |first = Hilda |title = North Cornwall Reflections |publisher = Bossiney Books | year =  1992 | page = 28 |isbn = 0-948158-79-4 }}</ref> but it is unclear how old the tradition is or when this ceased.

Boscastle was once a centre for slate quarrying which remained a viable industry until around the turn of the 20th century. The remains of four [[Boscastle Slate Quarries|quarries]] are situated in the cliffs between Boscastle Harbour and [[Trevalga]].

===Churches===
The Rector of Boscastle is responsible for seven churches in the district: [[Forrabury and Minster|Forrabury (St Symphorian), Minster (St Merthiana)]], [[St Juliot]], [[Lesnewth]] (St Michael and All Angels), [[Trevalga]] (St Petroc), [[Otterham]] (St Denis) and [[Davidstow]] (St David).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.boscastlecornwall.org.uk/church_locations.htm |title=Boscastle group of 7 Churches |work=Village website |access-date=26 December 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080723154606/http://www.boscastlecornwall.org.uk/church_locations.htm |archive-date=23 July 2008 |df=dmy }}</ref> St Juliot is of particular interest to devotees of the works of [[Thomas Hardy]] since he acted as the architect for the church's [[Victorian restoration|restoration]] in March 1870 and this is where he met his first wife, [[Emma Gifford]], who was the Rector's sister-in-law. Their love affair was the inspiration for his novel ''[[A Pair of Blue Eyes]]'' and, later in life, some of his poetry.

;''A Seaside Parish''
In 2004 British television channel [[BBC 2]] began broadcasting ''[[A Seaside Parish]]'', a weekly series focusing on the life of the newly appointed Rector of Boscastle, Christine Musser.<ref>{{cite news | url= https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/cornwall/3445601.stm | work= BBC News | title= Seaside priest is TV star | date= 1 February 2004 | access-date= 25 August 2008}}</ref>

=== Tourism===
The village, with its picturesque harbour, is a popular tourist destination. Among the attractions are the [[Museum of Witchcraft]], Uncle Paul's Emporium, the Boscastle pottery shop, and access to the [[South West Coast Path]].

Much of the land in and around Boscastle is owned by the [[National Trust]], including both sides of the harbour, Forrabury Stitches, high above the Boscastle and divided into ancient "[[stitchmeal farming|stitchmeal]]" cultivation plots, and large areas of the [[Valency Valley]], known for its connections to [[Thomas Hardy]].

The former harbour stables (part of the National Trust estate) are now a [[youth hostel]] run by [[YHA (England and Wales)|YHA]], popular with walkers. The National Trust runs a shop at the harbour,<ref>[http://www.visitboscastleandtintagel.com/boscastle-and-tintagel/thedms.asp?dms=13&venue=4520516]{{dead link|date=May 2015}}</ref> and a [[visitor centre]] in the Old Smithy.

[[Charles III]], then Prince of Wales, visited Boscastle on 15 July 2019 to commemorate the anniversary of the Cornwall AONB and to visit a local [[Cornish hedge]] restoration project.<ref>Rosie Cripps [http://www.camelford-today.co.uk/article.cfm?id=113141&searchyear=2019  Warm welcome for Prince Charles as he visits Boscastle ]; ''Camelford & Delabole Post''; 16 July 2019</ref>

The Boscastle Breakdown [[step dance]], The Boscastle & Tintagel Players concertinas, cello & stepping is included in the Topic Records compilation ''[[The Voice of the People]]''.{{clarify|date=October 2023}}

The Wellington Inn is a 16th-century coaching inn near the harbour; its furnishings include church lamps which were donated by the architect [[Thomas Hardy]] and stained glass windows installed in 1846.<ref>Protz, Roger (2000) ''Britain's 500 Best Pubs''. London: Carlton Books {{ISBN|978-1-85868-826-8}}; p. 279</ref>

===Boscastle floods===
{{main|Boscastle flood of 2004}}
;Flood of 2004
A [[Boscastle flood, 2004|flash flood]] on 16 August 2004 caused extensive damage to the village. Residents were trapped in houses, on roofs, in cars, and on the river's banks, and the village's visitor centre was washed away.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/cornwall/3570940.stm |title=UK | England | Cornwall | Dozens rescued from flash floods |publisher=News.bbc.co.uk |date=17 August 2004 |access-date=9 May 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.metoffice.gov.uk/climate/uk/interesting/20040816.html |title=Flooding in north Cornwall - 16 August 2004 |publisher=Metoffice.gov.uk |access-date=9 May 2015}}</ref>
Two [[Royal Air Force]] [[Westland Sea King]] rescue helicopters from [[Royal Marines Base Chivenor|Chivenor]], three [[Royal Navy]] Sea Kings from [[Culdrose]], one RAF Sea King from [[RAF St. Mawgan|St Mawgan]] and one Coastguard S61 helicopter from [[Portland, Dorset|Portland]] searched for and assisted casualties in and around the village. The operation was coordinated by the [[Aeronautical Rescue Coordination Centre]] based at [[RAF Kinloss]] in [[Scotland]] in the largest peacetime rescue operation ever launched in the UK. A total of 91 people were rescued, with no fatalities.

The cause of the flooding was over {{convert|60|mm}} of rainfall (typically a month's rainfall) falling in two hours  due to thunderstorms developing on a [[Convergence zone|convergence line]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Weatherwatch: a meeting of winds in convergence zones |last=Wooltorton |first=Jodie |newspaper=The Guardian |date=17 August 2021 |url= https://www.theguardian.com/news/2021/aug/17/weatherwatch-a-meeting-of-winds-in-convergence-zones}}</ref> The ground was already saturated due to the previous two weeks of above average rainfall; the drainage basin has many steep slopes, and has areas of impermeable slate causing rapid surface run-off. Boscastle is at the [[confluence]] of two rivers, Valency and Jordan;<ref>The names Jordan and Paradise may have been borrowed from the Bible by a reinterpretation of the French "jardin", i.s.the garden of Bottreaux Castle; Armstrong, W. J. C. (1931) ''A Rambler's Guide to Boscastle''; 2nd ed. Boscastle: the author; p. 10</ref> a large quantity of water arrived within a short space of time, causing the rivers to overflow. The flooding coincided with a high tide, worsening the storm's impact.

Around 50 cars were swept into the harbour and the bridge was washed away, roads were submerged under {{convert|2.75|m|ft|0}} of water, making communication effectively impossible until flood-waters subsided. The sewerage system burst, so for a range of health and safety reasons Boscastle was declared temporarily inaccessible. Homes, businesses and cars belonging to more than 1,000 people were swept away; income from tourism was lost, which affected livelihoods and the local economy; there were vast numbers of subsequent insurance claims.{{citation needed|date=October 2023}}

;Flood of 2007
Boscastle was flooded again on 21 June 2007 although the scale of destruction was not nearly as serious as in 2004.

==Sport==
Boscastle Golf Club (now defunct) was founded in 1907. The club continued until the mid-1920s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.golfsmissinglinks.co.uk/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1013 |title=Golfs Missing Links |publisher=Golfsmissinglinks.co.uk |access-date=9 May 2015}}</ref>

Boscastle and Crackington Pilot Gig Club formed in 2004 and row from Boscastle harbour, [[Port Gaverne]] and [[Upper Tamar Lake]]. They have three gigs; ''Torrent'' (named after the 2004 floods). ''Rival'' and ''Golden Gear''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Boscastle & Crackington |url=https://www.gigrower.co.uk/boscastle-and-crackington-gig-club/ |website=GigRower |access-date=2 October 2021}}</ref>

[[Cornish wrestling]] prize tournaments, were held in Boscastle in the 19th century.<ref name="WT07071838">Western Times, 7 July 1838.</ref>

600354.title: Quarry Bank Mill
600354.extract:
Quarry Bank Mill (also known as Styal Mill) in Styal, Cheshire, England, is one of the best preserved textile factories of the Industrial Revolution.  Built in 1784, the cotton mill is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade II* listed building. Quarry Bank Mill was established by Samuel Greg, and was notable for innovations both in machinery and also in its approach to labour relations, the latter largely as a result of the work of Greg's wife, Hannah Lightbody. The family took a somewhat paternalistic attitude toward the workers, providing medical care for all and limited education to the children, but all laboured roughly 72 hours per week until 1847 when a new law shortened the hours.
Greg also built housing for all of his workers, in a large community now known as Styal Estate. Some were conversions of farm houses, or older residences but 42 new cottages, including the Oak Cottages (now Grade II Listed), were built in the 1820s when the mill was being expanded.
The National Trust, which runs the mill and Styal Estate as a museum that is open to the public, calls the site "one of Britain's greatest industrial heritage sites, home to a complete industrial community". According to the Council of Europe, the mill with Styal village make up "the most complete and least altered factory colony of the Industrial Revolution. It is of outstanding national and international importance".

The family took a somewhat paternalistic attitude toward the workers, providing medical care for all and limited education to the children, but all laboured roughly 72 hours per week until 1847 when a new law shortened the hours.{{Cite web |url=https://hannahbarker.net/ |title=Historical Guide to the Apprentice House, Quarry Bank Professor Hannah Barker, U of Manchester |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=28 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210228013348/https://hannahbarker.net/ |url-status=dead }}{{Cite web |url=https://hannahbarker.net/2019/10/19/historical-guide-to-styal-village-and-13-oak-cottages/ |title=Professor Hannah Barker, U of Manchester |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=19 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119021748/https://hannahbarker.net/2019/10/19/historical-guide-to-styal-village-and-13-oak-cottages/ |url-status=dead }} Greg also built housing for all of his workers, in a large community now known as Styal Estate. It is of outstanding national and international importance".{{cite web |url=https://www.erih.net/i-want-to-go-there/site/quarry-bank-mill |title=Quarry Bank Mill |work=European Route of Industrial Heritage |publisher=Council of Europe |access-date=23 June 2021}} ==Location== Quarry Bank Mill is on the outskirts of [[Styal]] in [[Cheshire]], abutting and to the south of [[Manchester Airport]]. The mill is on the bank of the [[River Bollin]], which provided water to power the waterwheels. It was connected by road to the [[Bridgewater Canal]] for transporting raw cotton from the port of Liverpool.{{sfn|Westall|1994|loc=Illustration 59}} The site consisted of three farms or folds. [[Styal railway station]] opened in 1909, about a {{convert|1/3|mi|km}} away.{{Google Maps|url=https://www.google.com/maps/place/National+Trust+-+Quarry+Bank/@53.3476763,-2.2437787,1126m|title=National Trust - Quarry Bank}} ==History== [[Samuel Greg]] leased land at Quarrell Hole on Pownall Fee from Lord Stamford, who imposed a condition that "none of the surrounding trees should be pruned, felled or lopped"; maintaining the woodland character of the area. One reason for selecting this location was the "suitable head of water provided by the River Bollin and its proximity to the Bridgewater Canal and thus Liverpool". The factory was built in 1784 by Greg{{cite web|url=http://www.spinningtheweb.org.uk/m_display.php?irn=35&sub=rural&theme=places&crumb=Quarry+Bank+Mill|title=Quarry Bank Mill history|access-date=25 September 2007|archive-date=24 December 2012|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224063540/http://www.spinningtheweb.org.uk/m_display.php?irn=35&sub=rural&theme=places&crumb=Quarry+Bank+Mill|url-status=dead}} to [[spinning (textiles)|spin]] cotton. When Greg retired in 1832, it was the largest such business in the United Kingdom. The water-powered Georgian mill still produces cotton [[Calico (fabric)|calico]]. The Gregs were careful and pragmatic, paternalistic mill owners, and the mill underwent expansion and change throughout its history. When Greg's son, [[Robert Hyde Greg]], took over the business, he introduced [[weaving]]. Samuel Greg died in 1834. An 1835 report provided these specifics about the mill: "It is driven by an elegant water-wheel, thirty-two feet in diameter, and twenty-four feet broad, equivalent in power to one hundred and twenty horses"[https://europepmc.org/backend/ptpmcrender.fcgi?accid=PMC1037937&blobtype=pdf QUARRY BANK MILL BY ROBERT MURRAY, British Journal of Industrial Medicine, 4 September 1957] The Mill was attacked during the [[1842 General Strike|Plug Plot riots]] on 10 August 1842.{{Cite news|date=20 August 1842|title=The Disturbances in the Manufacturing Districts|page=232|work=Illustrated London News|url=https://www.iln.org.uk/iln_years/year/1842%20aug%2020%20riots%202.html|access-date=3 October 2020}} The mill's iron [[water wheel]], the fourth to be installed, was designed by [[Thomas Hewes]] and built between 1816 and 1820. Overhead shafts above the machines were attached to the water wheel by a belt. When the wheel turned, the motion moved the belt and powered the machinery. A beam engine and a horizontal steam engine were subsequently installed to supplement the power. The Hewes wheel broke in 1904, but the River Bollin continued to power the mill through two water turbines. The mill owners purchased a Boulton and Watt steam engine in 1810 and a few years later acquired another, as the river's water level was often low in the summer, which could interrupt cloth production for several years. Steam engines could produce power all year round. Today the mill houses the most powerful working waterwheel in Europe, an iron wheel moved from [[Glasshouses Mill]] at [[Pateley Bridge]] designed by [[Sir William Fairbairn]] who had been Hewes' apprentice. ===Mill community=== The sparse accommodation that existed when the Gregs built the mill was soon exhausted, and Greg built plain cottages, including the Oak Cottages, which are now Grade II listed; these were rented to his workers. Each house had a parlour, kitchen and two bedrooms (a [[two-up two-down]]), an outside privy and a small garden. Rent was deducted from the workers' wages.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=155}} The area of worker housing became known as Styal Estate. [[File:Oak Cottages, Styal (2).jpg|thumb|Part of the Oak Cottages at Styal]] The Gregs owned a home in Manchester but also built a home near the mill in 1797, called "Quarry Bank House".[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quarry-bank/features/samuel-greg-of-quarry-bank Samuel Greg and the beginnings of Quarry Bank] The building has been Grade II listed since 1975.[https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1237686 Quarry Bank House, List Entry Number 1237686] It was restored in 2017 in a manner that ensured that "all primary features dating from the Greg family’s occupation have been retained", and was opened to visits by the public by the National Trust.{{Cite web |url=https://buttress.net/project/quarry-bank-mill/ |title=Quarry Bank |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=23 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210123050519/https://buttress.net/project/quarry-bank-mill/ |url-status=dead }}[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quarry-bank/projects/step-inside-quarry-bank-house Step inside Quarry Bank House] Samuel Greg, like [[Robert Owen]], who built [[New Lanark]], attempted to bring the structured order of a country village to his new industrial centres. He built Oak School to educate the children and the [[Norcliffe Chapel]] where the villagers worshipped and held a [[Sunday school]].{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|pp=155–7}} [[File:Cottages and path, Styal village - geograph.org.uk - 416390.jpg|thumb|Workers' cottages at Styal Estate]] At first, Greg converted farm buildings in Styal to house workers. As the mill increased in size, new housing was constructed for the workers.{{cite web|url=http://www.manchester2002-uk.com/history/victorian/quarrybankmill.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020216000025/http://www.manchester2002-uk.com/history/victorian/quarrybankmill.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=16 February 2002|title=Styal Village|access-date=25 September 2007}} According to the National Trust, in the 1820s, "... new terraced cottages brought a brand new style of architecture and an expanding population ... In the tiny two-up-two-down cottages workers lived in cramped conditions, with as many as 14 people living in one house and tenants sub-letting rooms to other mill workers".[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quarry-bank/features/discover-the-stories-of-the-workers-in-styal-village Discover the stories of the workers in Styal village] The Gregs also built the village shop and, for roughly five decades, remained the owners. Medical care for mill workers was provided by staff physicians and surgeons.{{Cite web |url=https://www.inpursuitofplants.co.uk/post/ep3-the-natural-world-of-quarry-bank-mill |title=Ep3: The Natural World of Quarry Bank Mill |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=21 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121143817/https://www.inpursuitofplants.co.uk/post/ep3-the-natural-world-of-quarry-bank-mill |url-status=dead }} The mill provided the "earliest recorded occupational health service in this country", according to an article in the [[British Journal of Industrial Medicine]].[https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Peter-Holland%3A-a-pioneer-of-occupational-medicine.-Murray/b9951185482706b5b398a23a32bbdaf6599f1b9d Peter Holland: a pioneer of occupational medicine, R Murray] ===Apprentice system=== [[File:Apprentice House, Quarry Bank Mill - geograph.org.uk - 734182.jpg|thumb|The Apprentice House where up to 90 children lived]] Quarry Bank Mill employed [[Child labour#History|child apprentices]], a system that continued only until 1847. Most were children of families in poverty, living in [[workhouse]]s, which sent them to the mill which was "clamouring for cheap labour". At the time, the consensus was that the children were better off in labour than they would have been under 'the step-motherly care of the Poor Law'", according to a reliable source.Examination of Thomas Priestly, 2 August 1806, Manchester Central Reference Library, C5/8/9/5 (1806) Initially, the children were brought from Hackney and Chelsea but by 1834 they came mostly from neighbouring parishes or Liverpool poorhouses.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=155}} The last child to be indentured started work in 1841. Child labour constituted over half of the labour force in the early decades of the mill's operation, according to Prof Hannah Barker, chair of Manchester Histories at the [[University of Manchester]]. "By 1833 apprentices made up only 20% of workforce at Styal, and in 1847 the apprentice system was completely abandoned".{{Cite web |url=https://hannahbarker.net/ |title=Historical Guide to the Apprentice House, Quarry Bank |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=28 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210228013348/https://hannahbarker.net/ |url-status=dead }} The first children apprentices lived in lodgings in the neighbourhood, then in 1790 Greg built the [[Apprentice House, Quarry Bank Mill|Apprentice House]] near the factory.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=155}} Greg believed he could get the best out of his workers by treating them fairly. He hired a superintendent to attend to their care and morals, and members of the Greg family and external tutors gave them lessons.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=155}} Some of the work was dangerous, with fingers sometimes being severed by the machines.{{sfn|Bourne|2007|p=27}} Samuel Greg employed Peter Holland, father of the Royal Physician [[Sir Henry Holland, 1st Baronet]] and uncle of [[Elizabeth Gaskell]], as mill doctor. Holland was responsible for the health of the children and other workers, and was the first doctor to be employed in such a capacity.[https://www.jstor.org/stable/27727441?seq=1 Peter Holland: A Pioneer of Occupational Medicine] Life for the children was not ideal, of course. Hours were long: 12 hours per day, six days a week, according to documents from 1794.[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quarry-bank/features/rights-of-the-child-exhibition Rights of the Child exhibition] Time for play was allowed only on Sunday afternoons. Still, their "diet appears to have been a relatively good one", according to Professor Barker's research, and some education was provided. (The Gregs were [[Unitarianism|Unitarians]] who believed in educating their workers, including Sunday School for both sexes.) Initially, schooling was provided only for boys, for an hour on three evenings of the week, at most; by 1833 the mill claimed that girls were also getting some education on Sunday afternoons.{{Cite web |url=https://hannahbarker.net/2015/12/05/hard-work-and-hellfire-educating-the-children-at-apprentice-house/ |title=Hard work and hellfire: educating the children at Apprentice House, Prof Hannah Barker, U of Manchester |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=27 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227234752/https://hannahbarker.net/2015/12/05/hard-work-and-hellfire-educating-the-children-at-apprentice-house/ |url-status=dead }} A comparative study of child mill workers of the era by Katrina Honeyman indicated that "those at Quarry Bank were treated 'better than average', but that the Gregs were not amongst the best employers in the country".{{Cite web |url=https://hannahbarker.net/ |title=Historical Guide to the Apprentice House, Quarry Bank, Prof Hannah Barker, U of Manchester |access-date=2 March 2021 |archive-date=28 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210228013348/https://hannahbarker.net/ |url-status=dead }} A former director of the Quarry Bank Mill, and author of a book about Hannah Greg, provided this summary of child labour, based on extensive research.[https://www.greatbritishlife.co.uk/homes-and-gardens/places-to-live/the-true-story-behind-quarry-bank-mill-the-inspiration-for-7114400 The true story behind Quarry Bank Mill the inspiration for the Channel 4 drama]
Over half of Samuel Greg’s workforce were poor and orphaned children ... the children were given good medical care by the Greg family doctor, and education in writing and maths three nights a week ... although the child workers were not subjected to corporal punishment, bad behaviour brought overtime, threats that girls would have their heads shaved or young workers being locked in a room for days on a porridge-only diet".
===20th and 21st century=== The estate and mill were eventually inherited by Robert Hyde Greg and then by Alexander Carlton Greg, who donated the site in 1939 to the [[National Trust]].[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quarry-bank/features/the-history-of-quarry-bank-mill the Greg Family] The mill continued in production until 1959. According to the historic listing, the {{convert|32|ft|m|adj=on}} diameter waterwheel was replaced by two turbines in 1904. Some restoration was completed in 1969.[https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1237687 Quarry Bank Mill] In 2006, the National Trust acquired Quarry Bank House and its gardens, and in 2010 the gardener's house and the upper gardens.National Trust Magazine, Spring 2013 In 2013 the mill received 130,000 visitors. In 2013, the trust launched an appeal to raise £1.4 million to restore a worker's cottage, a shop and the Greg's glasshouses and digitise records relating to Gregs and the mill workers.[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-manchester-21424159 BBC News: Project to restore Quarry Bank Mill in Cheshire] (accessed 12 February 2013) During 2015–2020, the Quarry Bank Project improved the site for visitors with a £9.4 million restoration. "New areas have been restored and for the first time ever visitors can now explore the complete industrial heritage site at Quarry Bank".[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quarry-bank/features/the-quarry-bank-project-2014-2019 The Quarry Bank Project 2015–2020] A promotional video published by the Trust depicts scenes and activities that visitors can experience.[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8TOI1Fh8kgo Quarry Bank Mill, The National Trust 2 May 2019] ==Architecture== [[File:Quarry Bank Mill - geograph.org.uk - 793912.jpg|thumb|right|Front elevation of Quarry Bank Mill]] Quarry Bank is an example of an early, rural, cotton-spinning mill that was initially dependent on water power. The first mill was built by Samuel Greg and John Massey in 1784. Its design was functional and unadorned, growing out of the pragmatism of the men who felt no need to make a bold architectural statement.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=161}} It was a four-storey mill measuring {{convert|8.5|m|ft|order=flip}} by {{convert|27.5|m|ft|order=flip}}, with an attached staircase, counting house and warehouse. It was designed to use [[water frame]]s, which had just come out of patent, and the increased supply of cotton caused by the cessation of the [[American War of Independence]]. The water wheel was at the north end of the mill. The mill was extended in 1796 when it was doubled in length and a fifth floor added. A second wheel was built at the southern end. The mill was extended between 1817 and 1820, and a mansard-roofed wing was added to part of the 1796 building forward, beneath which the wheel was installed. The new building kept the 1784 detailing with respect to line and windows.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=}} The 1784 mill ran 2425 spindles. After 1805, with the new wheel, it ran 3452 spindles.{{sfn|Bourne|2007|p=12}} Weaving sheds were added in 1836 and 1838, and they were of two storeys and housed 305 looms.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|pp=123–-127, 134}} Before the 1830s, spinning mills produced cotton, that was [[Putting-out system|put-out]] to [[hand-loom]] weavers who worked in their own homes or small [[loom shop]]s, like the one Greg owned at [[Eyam]].{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=38}} Hand-loom weaving continued in parallel to [[power loom]] weaving throughout the 19th century. Around 1830, the power loom became sufficiently viable for independent [[weaving shed]]s to be set up, and for larger owners to add weaving sheds to their spinning mills. A weaving shed needed the correct light and humidity, and a floor that was stable enough to withstand the vibration caused by the picking of many looms. Quarry Bank Mill is of national significance in that it used two-storey side-lit buildings rather the a [[weaving shed|single storey shed]]s with a saw-tooth roof.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=123}} The first two-storey shed at Quarry Bank was {{convert|33|m|ft|order=flip}} by {{convert|6.5|m|ft|order=flip}}. The 1838 building was {{convert|30|m|ft|order=flip}} by {{convert|10|m|ft|order=flip}} to which a storey was added in 1842 for warping and beaming. In the Gregs pragmatic way, looms were purchased gradually.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=124}} ===Water power=== [[File:Quarry Bank Mill waterwheel 1.webm|thumb|right|The waterwheel rotating]] The first wheel was a wooden [[overshot wheel]] taking water by means of a long leat from upstream on the River Bollin. The second wheel built by Peter Ewart in 1801 was wooden. To increase power, he dammed the Bollin and took water into the mill directly, the [[tailrace]] leaving the river below the dam. The third wheel of 1807 was a replacement for one of the wooden wheels.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=61}} It is believed it was a [[waterwheel#Suspension wheels and rim-gears|suspension wheel]], {{convert|8|m|ft|order=flip}} in diameter made from iron to the design of [[Thomas Hewes]].{{sfn|Bourne|2007|p=12}} The fourth wheel, the ''Great Wheel'' was also designed by Hewes. The challenge was to increase the head of water acting on the wheel while using the same volume of water. It was achieved by sinking the wheel pit to below the level of the river and taking the tail race through a tunnel a kilometre downstream to rejoin the Bollin at Giant's Castle. This gave a head of {{convert|32|ft|m}} acting on the {{convert|32|ft|m}} diameter suspension wheel- which is {{convert|21|ft|m}} wide. The ''Great Wheel'' operated from 1818 to 1871 when the mill pool had silted up, and then to 1904.{{sfn|Bourne|2007|pp=13,14}} In 1905, two [[water turbines]] built by Gilbert Gilkes and Company were installed to replace the ''Great Wheel''. They used the same head and tail race and operated until 1959.{{sfn|Bourne|2007|p=13}} When the mill was restored in 1983, a {{convert|25|ft|m}} diameter waterwheel of similar design to that of Hewes by his pupil Sir [[William Fairbairn]], was moved from [[Glasshouses, North Yorkshire|Glasshouses Mill]] near [[Pateley Bridge]] and installed to provide power to work the machinery. ===Steam power=== Water flow from the Bollin was unreliable, so an auxiliary steam engine was procured in 1810.{{sfn|Calladine|Fricker|1993|p=61}} It was a 10 hp [[beam engine]] from [[Boulton and Watt]]. In 1836 with the arrival of [[power loom]]s a second 20 hp Boulton and Watt beam engine was acquired. The first [[stationary steam engine|horizontal condensing engine]] was acquired in 1871. A new engine house was built. In 1906 the 1871 engine was replaced by a second-hand 60 hp engine.{{sfn|Bourne|2007|pp=14–15}} The engines no longer exist, and the museum has purchased a similar steam engine to display. ==Profiting from the slave trade== The Gregs were involved in the [[triangular trade]]. Samuel Greg's brother-in-law, Thomas Hodgson, owned a slave ship; his father, Thomas Greg, and his brother, John Greg, part-owned [[sugar plantation]]s on the Caribbean island of [[Dominica]]. The best documented is Hillsborough Estate, Dominica, which Samuel Greg and his brother Thomas inherited in 1795.{{cite web|title=The Greg family of Styal {{!}} Revealing Histories|url=http://revealinghistories.org.uk/why-was-cotton-so-important-in-north-west-england/people/the-greg-family-of-styal.html|website=revealinghistories.org.uk|publisher=8 Greater Manchester Museums|access-date=8 October 2017|language=en}} In 1818, it had 71 male and 68 female slaves.{{sfn|Bourne|2007|p=19}}{{Cite web |url=http://janus.lib.cam.ac.uk/db/node.xsp?id=EAD%2FGBR%2F0115%2FRCMS%20266 |title=› Domenica Estates Janus Repositories, University of Cambridge |access-date=2 April 2014 |archive-date=7 April 2014 Greg did not rely on Caribbean estate earnings to finance entry into cotton spinning, his interest in plantations formed part of a wider family engagement in commerce that included significant slave-related business".[https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lbs/person/view/2146644249 Samuel Greg Profile & Legacies Summary] "Samuel Greg ... his father Thomas and uncle John had interests in four estates in Dominica and St Vincent, ... while Samuel and his brother Thomas inherited the Hillsborough plantation in Dominica and other estates", according to a news 2406412.title: Glendurgan Garden
2406412.extract:
Glendurgan Garden (Cornish: Glynn Dowrgeun, meaning deep valley of otters) is a National Trust garden situated above the hamlet of Durgan on the Helford River and near  Mawnan Smith, in the civil parish of Mawnan, Cornwall, England, United Kingdom.
Glendurgan Garden was laid out by Alfred Fox in the 1820s and 1830s. In 1962 Glendurgan Garden was given to the National Trust by Cuthbert and Philip Fox.
The garden is notable for a cherry laurel maze, created in 1833.

'''Glendurgan Garden''' ({{langx|kw|'''Glynn Dowrgeun'''}}, meaning ''deep valley of otters'') is a [[National Trust]] garden situated above the hamlet of [[Durgan]] on the [[Helford River]] and near  [[Mawnan Smith]], in the civil parish of [[Mawnan]], [[Cornwall]], [[England]], [[United Kingdom]].

Glendurgan Garden was laid out by Alfred Fox in the 1820s and 1830s. In 1962 Glendurgan Garden was given to the National Trust by Cuthbert and Philip Fox.

The garden is notable for a [[cherry laurel]] [[maze]], created in 1833.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gardenvisit.com/gardens/glendurgan_garden|title = Glendurgan Garden}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2018/may/08/glendurgan-garden-cornwall-national-trust-family-day-trip|title = Glendurgan Garden, Cornwall: 'At every turn there is something unexpected to discover' – review|website = [[TheGuardian.com]]|date = 8 May 2018}}</ref>

2839033.title: Botallack Mine
2839033.extract: The Botallack Mine (Cornish: Bostalek) is a former mine in Botallack in the west of Cornwall, UK. Since 2006 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site – Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape. The mine is within the Aire Point to Carrick Du Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and the South West Coast Path passes along the cliff.

The '''Botallack Mine''' ({{langx|kw|Bostalek}}){{Citation needed|date=November 2023|reason=No source; "Botallack" is already Cornish.}} is a former mine in [[Botallack]] in the west of [[Cornwall]], UK. Since 2006 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site – [[Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape]]. The mine is within the [[Aire Point to Carrick Du SSSI|Aire Point to Carrick Du]] [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI) and the [[South West Coast Path]] passes along the cliff.

==Location==
The village of Botallack is on the [[B3306 road]], in a former [[Mining in Cornwall and Devon|tin and copper mining]] area between the town of [[St Just in Penwith]] and the village of [[Pendeen]].<ref>{{cite map |title=OS Explorer 102 Land's End |date=2015 |publisher=Ordnance Survey |location=Southampton |isbn=978 0 319 24304 6}}</ref>

==History==
Botallack was a submarine mine with tunnels extending under the sea, in places for half a mile. Over its recorded lifetime the mine produced around 14,500 tonnes of [[tin]], 20,000 tonnes of [[copper]], and 1,500 tonnes of [[arsenic]]. An estimated 1.5 million tonnes of [[Tailings|waste]] would have been dug up with the minerals.<ref name="Trust"/> It is unclear how far back mining activity goes in this location. Early records date from the 1500s. Some archaeological evidence points to mining here in the [[Roman Empire|Roman era]] or even as far back as the [[Bronze Age]].<ref name="Trust">{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/botallack |title=Botallack |publisher=National Trust |access-date=3 December 2016}}</ref>

Nicholas Boynes was captain of the mine in the early 18th-century and opened a "deep adit level", which was driven to the Corpus Christi lode in the higher mine. The first steam-engine was put to work at [[Carnyorth|Carnyorth Moor]] (later part of the Botallack [[Mining Sett|sett]]) in either 1795 or about 1810, depending on the source. In the first half of the 19th-century, the average price of Botallack tin was £64 4s a ton. The abolition of tin duty of 4s per 120 lbs to the [[Duke of Cornwall]] in 1838 helped to keep the mine operating despite a decline in the price of tin to £45 per ton.<ref name=Ouit>{{cite news |last1=Boynes (alias Ouit) |title=The Industries of Penzance and its Neighbourhood. No XX. The MIning of St. Just. I – History of the District |work=The Cornishman |issue=279 |date=15 November 1883 |page=6}}</ref> In the 1860s a new diagonal shaft was dug. A visit by the [[Edward VII|Prince]] and [[Alexandra of Denmark|Princess of Wales]] in 1865, when they descended the shaft, created a mini-boom in tourism, causing the mine operators to charge visitors a guinea per person.<ref name="Trust"/>

An increasing supply of tin – initially from [[Malaysia]], [[Banka Island]], and [[Sumatra]], and in the 1870s onwards from Australia – along with a fall in demand for tinplate in the American market, caused the price of tin to fall, causing many Cornish mines to close.<ref name=Ouit/> The managers decided in January 1883 to stop the Botallack and Crowns engines, because the number of men employed below ground was not sufficient to meet the costs of keeping the engines going.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Stoppage Of Part Of Botallack |work=The Cornishman |issue=236 |date=18 January 1883 |page=5}}</ref> On 2 October 1883 the recently renewed setts, which extended over {{Convert|2|mile}} – comprising Wheal Cock, the Crowns, Carnyorth and Higher Mine – were put up for auction as a "going concern". It included four pumping and three winding engines, two steam stamps, plus other appliances. At the auction it was stated that the mine ″... only needs from £20,000 to £25,000 to be put in good working order, ...″ There were no bids for the mine.<ref>{{cite news |title=Sale by Auction. Botallack, Cornwall |work=The Cornishman |issue=269 |date=6 September 1883 |page=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Botallack In The Market |work=The Cornishman |issue=273 |date=4 October 1883 |page=5}}</ref>

The following shafts were working in 1884,
* Botallack engine-shaft, {{convert|220|fathom}} deep and worked with a {{convert|30|inch}} cylinder 
* Crowns engine-shaft, {{convert|130|fathom}} deep and worked with a {{convert|36|inch}} cylinder
* Wheal Cock engine-shaft, {{convert|160|fathom}} deep and worked with a {{convert|30|inch}} cylinder
* Carnyorth engine-shaft, {{convert|130|fathom}} deep and worked with a {{convert|30|inch}} cylinder
* Wheal Cock skip-shaft, {{convert|170|fathom}} deep
* Botallack skip-shaft, {{convert|205|fathom}} deep 
* Carnyorth skip-shaft, {{convert|124|fathom}} deep
* Wheal Hazzard skip-shaft, {{convert|100|fathom}} deep
* Chy Cornish skip-shaft, {{convert|100|fathom}} deep

* Boscawen diagonal-shaft, about {{convert|500|fathom}} long, perpendicular depth {{convert|240|fathom}} and {{convert|300|fathom}} under the sea
* Approximately 10 other shafts varying in depth from a few fathoms to {{convert|50|fathom}} deep.<ref name="cman297">{{cite news |last1=Boynes (alias Ouit) |title=The Industries of Penzance and its Neighbourhood. No XX. The Mines of St Just. 5-Botallack Mine. (concluded) |work=The Cornishman |issue=297 |date=20 March 1884 |page=6}}</ref>

Other engines,
* Botallack stamping-engine, {{convert|30|inch}} cylinder
* Carnyorth stamping-engine, {{convert|24|inch}} cylinder

* saw-mill, {{convert|14|inch}} cylinder
* air-compressor, {{convert|14|inch}} cylinder.

A total of 265 workers were employed and the wage was approximately £800 per month.<ref name="cman297"/>

The average monthly yield of the mine was about 19 tons of tin, 3 tons of copper and 4 tons of [[arsenic]].<ref name="cman297"/>

The mine closed in 1895 as a result of falling tin and copper prices.<ref name="Trust"/>

The mining developments around Botallack form part of the St Just mining district's successful inclusion in the [[Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape]] [[World Heritage Site]], which was inscribed in July 2006.<ref name="Trust"/>

==Description==
[[File:Arsenic labyrinth.jpg|thumb|Arsenic labyrinth at Botallack]]
The engine houses in the Crowns section of Botallack Mine are set low down the cliffs north of Botallack. There are two engine houses and the remains of another pair on the cliff slopes above; the mine extends for about 400 metres out under the [[Atlantic]] ocean; the deepest shaft is 250 fathoms (about 500 metres) below sea level. The workings of Botallack Mine extend inland as far as the St Just to St Ives road, and at times included Wheal Cock further to the north-east.

The mine buildings on Botallack Cliffs are protected by the [[National Trust]]. There are two arsenic works opposite the Botallack Mine count house. At the top of the cliffs there is also the remains of one of the mine's arsenic-refining works.<ref>{{cite web |title=Seven Man Made Wonders |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/southwest/botallack_mine_mm/index.shtml |website=BBC |access-date=3 December 2016}}</ref>

The mineral [[Botallackite]] has its [[type locality (geology)|type locality]] here.<ref>{{cite web |title=Botallackite |url=http://www.mindat.org/min-732.html |website=mindat.org |publisher=Hudson Institute of Mineralogy |access-date=3 December 2016}}</ref>

==Popular culture==
[[File:James Clarke Hook (1819-1907) - From under the Sea - 1891.8 - Manchester Art Gallery.jpg|thumb|upright|''[[From Under the Sea]]'' by [[James Clarke Hook]], 1864]]
The mine is the setting for [[R. M. Ballantyne]]'s ''Deep Down''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ballantyne |first1=R. M. |title=Deep Down |date=2007 |publisher=The Vision Forum, Inc. |location=San Antonio |isbn=9781934554104 |page=49}}</ref>

The 1970s [[BBC]] television series ''[[Poldark (1975 TV series)|Poldark]]'' was filmed partly in Botallack, using Manor Farm as [[Nampara]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Film & Television Locations in Cornwall |url=http://www.cornwall-calling.co.uk/film-tv-locations.htm |website=Cornwall Calling |access-date=3 December 2016}}</ref> More recently, filming for [[Poldark (2015 TV series)|the new ''Poldark'' series]] also took place here.<ref name="Trust"/>

3281716.title: Tatton Park
3281716.extract: Tatton Park is a historic estate in Cheshire, England, north of the town of Knutsford. It contains a mansion, Tatton Hall; a medieval manor house, Tatton Old Hall; Tatton Park Gardens, a farm and a deer park of 2,000 acres (8.1 km2).  It is a popular visitor attraction and hosts over a hundred events annually. The estate is owned by the National Trust and is managed under lease by Cheshire East Council. Since 1999, it has hosted North West England's annual Royal Horticultural Society flower show.

3388210.title: Cotehele
3388210.extract: Cotehele is a medieval house with Tudor additions, situated in the parish of Calstock in the east of Cornwall, England, and now belonging to the National Trust. It is a rambling granite and slate-stone manor house on the banks of the River Tamar that has been little changed over five centuries. It was built by the Edgecumbe family in 1485 after the original Manor House was pulled down. Sir Richard Edgecumbe came into the property after fighting for Henry Tudor in the Battle of Bosworth. He was gifted with money and the original Manor House and estate and then proceeded to build Cotehele.

'''Cotehele''' is a [[Medieval architecture|medieval]] house with [[Tudor architecture|Tudor]] additions, situated in the parish of [[Calstock]] in the east of [[Cornwall]], England, and now belonging to the [[National Trust]]. It is a rambling granite and slate-stone manor house on the banks of the [[River Tamar]] that has been little changed over five centuries. It was built by the Edgecumbe family in 1485 after the original Manor House was pulled down. Sir Richard Edgecumbe came into the property after fighting for Henry Tudor in the [[Battle of Bosworth]]. He was gifted with money and the original Manor House and estate and then proceeded to build Cotehele.

==History==
The house was acquired by William Edgcumbe through his marriage to Hilaria, heiress of Cotehele.<ref name="Cadell & Davies, London 1814">{{cite web |title=Parishes: Callington - St Columb Pages 51-67  Magna Britannia: Volume 3, Cornwall. |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/magna-britannia/vol3/pp51-67 |website=British History Online |publisher=Cadell & Davies, London 1814 |access-date=10 June 2023}}</ref> The house is one of the least altered of the Tudor houses in the United Kingdom. The outbuildings include a stone dovecote in a remarkable state of preservation.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Buildings of England, Cornwall, 2nd ed. |last=Pevsner |first=Nicholas |year=1970 |publisher=Penguin Books }}</ref>

For centuries a second home of the [[Earl of Mount Edgcumbe|Edgcumbe family]], hosting a royal visit  from King [[George III]] in 1788,<ref name="Cadell & Davies, London 1814"/> it was the first property to be accepted by the Treasury in payment of [[death duty]]. The house and estate are now under the care of the [[National Trust]].<ref name=architecture/>  Notable contents include the Cotehele cupboard<ref name="CoteheleCupboard">{{cite journal |title=The Cotehele Cupboard: An Elegy in Oak |url=https://regionalfurnituresociety.files.wordpress.com/2013/02/01-oconnor.pdf |journal=Regional Furniture |year=2014 |last=O'Connor |first=Tina |volume=28 |pages=1–27 |access-date=2017-07-11 }}</ref><ref name="CoteheleCupboard2">{{cite journal |title=The Cotehele Cupboard Revisited: One Cupboard or Two? |url=https://regionalfurnituresociety.files.wordpress.com/2013/02/02-bowett-cotehele.pdf |journal=Regional Furniture |year=2014 |last=Bowett |first=Adam |volume=28 |pages=30–39 |access-date=2017-09-26 }}</ref> and the [[Cotehele clock]]. The house contains many tapestries that came, along with much of the furniture, from [[Mount Edgcumbe House]]. Regrettably, some have had pieces cut out to fit them in their new locations.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hunt |first1=Rachel |title=Cotehele |date=2013 |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |isbn=978-1-84359-428-4 |page=15}}</ref>

==The site==
The house is a [[Listed building|Grade I listed]] building, having been so designated on 21 July 1951. The house was probably founded around 1300 and various alterations were made in the early fifteenth century. Sir Richard Edgcumbe seems to have been involved in the first phase of development from 1486 to 1489, with his son Sir Piers Edgcumbe taking over for the second phase, from 1489 to 1520.<ref name="NHLE">{{NHLE|desc=Cotehele House|num= 1140255 |accessdate=22 May 2020}}</ref>

The grounds stretch down to a [[quay]] on the [[River Tamar]] where there is an outpost of the [[National Maritime Museum]]. There are a number of formal gardens and a richly planted area in the valley; features include a medieval dovecote, a [[Stew pond|stewpond]], a Victorian summerhouse and the eighteenth century  [[Prospect Tower]].<ref name=architecture>{{cite web |url=https://www.architecture.com/FindAnArchitect/ArchitectPractices/ARBArchitecture/Projects/CoteheleManor-137657.aspx |title=Cotehele Manor |year=2012 |publisher=architecture.com |access-date=13 August 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160820045556/https://www.architecture.com/FindAnArchitect/ArchitectPractices/ARBArchitecture/Projects/CoteheleManor-137657.aspx |archive-date=20 August 2016 }}</ref> The gardens and parkland are listed as Grade II* on the [[National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens|Register of Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/940 |title=Cotehele, Tavistock, England |publisher=Parks and Gardens UK |access-date=13 August 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160813184330/http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/940 |archive-date=13 August 2016 }}</ref> The south west side of the estate is bordered by the Morden stream which joins the Tamar at the quay. The estate mill is fed by this stream. The mill was used to grind grain bought in Plymouth and brought up river on the barge ''Myrtle'', and also to drive a sawmill and a generator for electricity. The Grade II listed mill<ref>{{NHLE|desc=The Mill|num= 1158803 |accessdate=22 May 2020}}</ref> has been restored to working order, producing flour for use in the restaurant as well as for sale.<ref name="NT">{{cite book |last1=Hunt |first1=Rachel |title=Cotehele |date=2018 |publisher=National Trust |location=Swindon |isbn=978-1-84359-428-4 |page=50}}</ref>

In 2008 a 'Mother Orchard' of over 250 apple trees, mainly of West-country varieties, was planted. The 8 acre orchard site is divided into eating, culinary and cider varieties.<ref name="Orchard">{{cite news |last=Morris |first=Steven |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2008/nov/04/apples-orchards-national-trust-cotehele |title=New hope for Britain's ancient apples |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=2008-11-04 |access-date=2017-09-26 }}</ref>

==Nicholas Condy==
The artist [[Nicholas Condy]] (1793-1857) made watercolours and paintings of Cotehele and the 2nd and 3rd Earls of Mount Edgcumbe were his patrons. Condy's painting, ''The Court Dinner at Cotehele'', and watercolours of the outside of Cotehele are on display in [[Mount Edgcumbe House]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=A story in 100 objects |url=https://www.mountedgcumbe.gov.uk/visit/exhibitions/a-story-in-100-objects/ |access-date=2025-11-18 |website=Mount Edgcumbe |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Cotehele's chapels==
===Cotehele House Chapel===
In Cotehele, on the west side of Hall Court are the Vicarage and the chapel, the chapel is connected to the main building via a small passageway leading to the dining room. The patron saints are St. Katharine and [[St. Anne]]. The chapel is among the oldest rooms in the house, alongside the Great Hall. In the chapel, there is a very rare and the original clock, still in operation today, it dates back to the [[Tudor period]].

===Cotehele Woodland Chapel===
In the grounds of Cotehele, directly East of the House close to the [[River Tamar]], lies a peaceful, basic chapel. inside there are pews going around the walls, two minister's benches and a very ornate table. the patron saints of the chapel are [[St George]] and St  [[Thomas Becket]]. The chapel was built by Sir [[Richard Edgcumbe (died 1489)]] between 1485 and 1489 as a thanksgiving for his escape from forces loyal to [[Richard III of England|Richard III]] in 1483.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ross|first=David|date=|title=Cotehele, Chapel in the Woods|url=https://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=4310|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-13|website=Britain Express|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100201044528/http://www.britainexpress.com:80/attractions.htm?attraction=4310 |archive-date=1 February 2010 }}</ref>

===The Edgcumbe Chapel===
'''The Edgcumbe Chapel''' is located in the East of the Northern aisle at St. Andrew's Church [[Calstock]], it contains two monuments of the late 17th- century: to Piers Edgcumbe (1666) and to [[Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich|Jemima, Countess of Sandwich]] (1674). it is no longer a chapel, but used by ministers to store religious items.

==Film location==
Cotehele was used in the filming of [[Trevor Nunn]]'s [[Twelfth Night (1996 film)|1996 film adaptation]] of ''[[Twelfth Night, or What You Will|Twelfth Night]]''. it was used for scenes taking place in the quayside tavern and the inside of Orsino's castle.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.visiting-cornwall.co.uk/locations.html |title=Twelfth Night |work=Locations around Cornwall (and the Isles of Scilly) that have been used in the making of films |publisher=Visiting Cornwall |access-date=13 August 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160731003345/http://www.visiting-cornwall.co.uk/locations.html |archive-date=31 July 2016 }}</ref>

3606323.title: Carnewas and Bedruthan Steps
3606323.extract:
Carnewas and Bedruthan Steps (Cornish: Karn Havos, meaning "rock-pile of summer dwelling" and Cornish: Bos Rudhen, meaning "Red-one's dwelling") is a stretch of coastline located on the north Cornish coast between Padstow and Newquay, in Cornwall, England, United Kingdom. It is within the parish of St Eval and is part-owned by the National Trust.
The trust maintains a shop and café, and the cliff–top views of rocks stretching into the distance along Bedruthan beach make the area a popular attraction for tourists and painters. The property affords walks along the South West Coast Path and the steep steps at Bedruthan allow access to a series of rocky beaches at low tide (not owned by the trust). Signs at the top of the steps down to the beaches warn visitors not to risk swimming in these waters due to heavy rips, fast tides, and submerged rocks.
A rockfall occurred in February 2020 affecting the lower steps and the safety netting on surrounding rocks resulting in closure of the steps.

[[File:Bedruthan Steps 22.jpg|thumb|right|240px|The Bedruthan Steps]]

'''Carnewas and Bedruthan Steps''' ({{langx|kw|Karn Havos}}, meaning "rock-pile of summer dwelling" and {{langx|kw|Bos Rudhen}}, meaning "Red-one's dwelling") is a stretch of [[coastline]] located on the north Cornish coast between [[Padstow]] and [[Newquay]], in [[Cornwall]], England, United Kingdom.<ref>Ordnance Survey: Landranger map sheet 200 ''Newquay & Bodmin'' {{ISBN|978-0-319-22938-5}}</ref> It is within the parish of [[St Eval]] and is part-owned by the [[National Trust]].
The trust maintains a shop and café, and the cliff–top views of rocks stretching into the distance along Bedruthan beach make the area a popular attraction for tourists and painters. The property affords walks along the [[South West Coast Path]] and the steep steps at Bedruthan allow access to a series of rocky beaches at low tide (not owned by the trust). Signs at the top of the steps down to the beaches warn visitors not to risk swimming in these waters due to heavy [[Rip current|rips]], fast tides, and submerged rocks.

A rockfall occurred in February 2020 affecting the lower steps and the safety netting on surrounding rocks resulting in closure of the steps.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/carnewas-at-bedruthan/features/steps-to-beach-closed |title= Steps to beach closed |date= Feb 2020 |publisher= National Trust |access-date= 24 May 2020 }}</ref>

==History==
People have been in the area since at least the [[Bronze Age Britain|Bronze Age]] with six [[Tumulus|barrows]] nearby to the north, and overlooking Bedruthan Steps is Redcliff Castle, which dates back to at least the [[Iron Age]]. Redcliff Castle has three ramparts divided by two ditches, part of which have been quarried to improve the defences. Much of the internal parts of the castle have been eroded by the sea. A second castle is within a mile to the north at Park Head and two miles to the south at Griffin's Point, a third. Cliff Castles or [[promontory fort]]s are defensive structures that are thought by archaeologists to have been permanently occupied.<ref name="Le Messurier">{{cite book|last=Le Messurier|first=Brian|title=Trevose to Watergate Bay including Bedruthan Steps (not NT)|year=1998|publisher=[[National Trust]]|pages=8}}</ref> In 2009, a ''[[menhir]]'' or longstone was discovered in a boundary hedge close to the coastpath. The stone lies on its side and is {{convert|9|ft|abbr=on}} long.<ref>{{cite web|last=Harper|first=Sheila|title=Carnewas Longstone – Standing Stone (Menhir)|url=http://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=25232|publisher=The Megalithic Portal|access-date=21 May 2012}}</ref>

Evidence of mining exists as shafts on the cliffs nearby at Trenance Point, and adits above the beach at Carnewas. Carnewas mine<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.aditnow.co.uk/Mines/Carnewas-Mixed-Mine_5278/#location |title= Carnewas Mixed Mine (United Kingdom) |date= 2020 |work= AditNow... the site for mine explorers and mining historians |publisher= aditnow.co.uk |access-date= 24 May 2020 |archive-date= 10 April 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210410144327/https://www.aditnow.co.uk/Mines/Carnewas-Mixed-Mine_5278/#location |url-status= dead }}</ref> itself started in 1855 and followed a [[lead]] lode accessible from near the tideline at low water with lodes containing [[silver]], [[copper]]/[[antimony]] ([[tetrahedrite]]) and [[nickel]] at a lower level.<ref name=mindat>{{cite web |url= https://www.mindat.org/loc-240610.html |title= Carnewas Mine, St Eval, Wadebridge District, Cornwall, England, UK |date= 2020 |work= mindat.org |publisher= mindat.org and the Hudson Institute of Mineralogy |access-date=24 May 2020 }}</ref> This working ceased operation in 1863 but the workings were opened again in 1868 to extract [[iron]] ([[hematite]]), closing in 1874 having produced over 6000 tons of [[iron ore]]<ref name=mindat /> although between 1871 and 1874 total production was only 940 tons{{Citation needed|date=May 2020}}. Ladders and steps to the beach are thought to have been needed to reach the mine workings. The National Trust shop was originally the count house (office) of Carnewas Mine, and the cafe was one of the mine buildings.

The name Bedruthan Steps is said to be taken from a mythological giant called Bedruthan, who used the rocks (stacks) on the beach as stepping stones, and seems to be a late-19th-century invention for Victorian tourists. The first written record of the name is from the [[The West Briton|West Briton]] newspaper in February 1847 and is likely to refer to one of two cliff staircases used by miners to get to the mine workings and now refers to the whole beach.<ref name="Le Messurier"/>

Each of the stacks has a name and from north to south they are Queen Bess, Samaritan Island, Redcove Island, Pendarves Island, and Carnewas Island. Queen Bess rock was so named as it was supposed to resemble the outline of [[Queen Elizabeth I]], although the head was lost after a storm in 1981.<ref name=landscapes>{{cite book |last = Darke |first = Jo |title = Cornish Landscapes |publisher = Opus books |year = 1983 |page = 55 |isbn = 0-7134-4187-9 }}</ref> Samaritan Island is named after a ship the ''Good Samaritan'', which was wrecked there in October 1846 with the loss of nine lives (another source states that the wreck occurred in 1850<ref name=landscapes />). A rhyme written at the time states, "The ''Good Samaritan'' came ashore, To feed the hungry and clothe the poor, With barrels of beef and bales of linen, No poor soul shall want for a shilling"<ref>{{cite book|last1=Pearce|first1=Cathryn J.|title=Cornish Wrecking, 1700-1860: Reality and Popular Myth|date=2010|publisher=Boydell & Brewer|isbn=9781843835554|page=91|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b1jL-ZvuLQ4C&dq=The+Good+Samaritan+came+ashore|access-date=7 February 2018}}</ref>

==Environment==
[[File:Bedruthan Steps from halfway point.jpg|thumb|Bedruthan Steps from halfway point]]
The section of coastline from Carnewas to [[Stepper Point]] is part of the [[Cornwall National Landscape]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cornwall-aonb.gov.uk/carnewastostepperpoint |title=04 carnewas to stepper point |publisher=cornwall-aonb.gov.uk |access-date=24 May 2020 }}{{Dead link|date=December 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and subject to special landscape protection.  In addition, Bedruthan Steps and Park Head is an {{convert|80.8|ha|adj=on|acre}} [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]], designated for its [[Geology of Cornwall|geological]] and [[Flora and fauna of Cornwall|biological]] interest in 1951. The site was subject to a revision in 1973 and renotified in 1986. It is noted for its [[slate]]s and [[fossils]] from the [[Devonian|Middle Devonian]], various [[moss]]es, and [[beetle]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bedruthan Steps and Park Head |url=http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1002099.pdf |publisher=[[Natural England]] |access-date=25 October 2011 |year=1986 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024211744/http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1002099.pdf |archive-date=24 October 2012 |df=dmy }}</ref> Bedruthan Steps is also a [[Geological Conservation Review]] site because it is a ″source of rare fish specimens″, which were first reported in 1848 by W Pengelly.<ref>{{cite web|title=Geological Conservation Review. Bedruthan Steps|url=https://jncc.gov.uk/jncc-assets/GCR/gcr-site-account-2246.pdf|publisher=JNCC|access-date=19 April 2025}}</ref>

;Flora
The coast here is exposed to westerly winds and the clifftops provide an exposed environment best suited to low-growing plants. Flowers to be found along the cost between [[Mawgan Porth]] and Bedruthan include [[Bird's foot trefoil]], [[Kidney vetch]], [[Jasione montana|Sheep's-bit]] and [[Spring squill]], plus the distinctly maritime species [[Armeria maritima|Sea Pink (Thrift)]] and [[Sea Campion]].<ref>{{cite web
|url= https://www.scarlethotel.co.uk/wildflower-cornwall-spring/ |title= Our beautiful, coastal spring wildflowers |author= Hannah Chapman |date= 7 May 2014 |publisher= Scarlet Hotel |access-date= 24 May 2020 }}</ref>

;Geology
The bedrock at Bedruthan Steps is at the northernmost extent of a series of sedimentary rocks classified as sandstone, siltstone and mudstone and known as the Bedruthan Formation.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://mapapps2.bgs.ac.uk/geoindex/home.html |title= Location 184815,69087 |date= 2019 |work= Geoindex onshore |publisher= British Geological Survey |access-date=24 May 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.bgs.ac.uk/lexicon/lexicon.cfm?pub=BEDN |title= Bedruthan Formation |date= 2020 |work=The BGS Lexicon of Named Rock Units |publisher= British Geological Survey |access-date=24 May 2020 }}</ref> The underlying rock from Bedruthan Steps to Trevose Head is Middle Devonian slates (386–377 Ma) with [[Gritstone|Staddon Grits]] to the south towards Trenance Point. The thickness of the slates have been estimated at over {{convert|2000|m|ft|abbr=on}}.
Marine erosion by the sea carrying sand and pebbles has worn away the weaker, softer rocks to leave the stacks seen today. Fossils of fish, [[coral]]s, [[trilobite]]s, etc. have been found in the [[Eifelian]] slates on Samaritan and Pendarves Islands.<ref name=Bristow>{{cite book|last=Bristow|first=Colin M|title=Cornwall's Geology and Scenery. An Introduction|year=1996|publisher=Cornish Hillside Publications|location=St Austell|isbn=1-900147-00-9}}</ref> Few fossils are useful for dating here, but one (although considered to be problematical) ''Pteroconus mirus'' dates the formations to the Eifelian.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Beese|first=A P|title=The argillite facies of the Middle Devonian succession in north Cornwall|journal=Proceedings of the Ussher Society|year=1982|volume=5|issue=3|url=http://ussher.org.uk/journal/80s/1982/documents/PUS_1982.pdf|access-date=15 December 2012|editor1-last=Power|editor1-first= G M |publisher=[[Ussher Society]] |location=Crediton |issn=0566-3954}}</ref> At the end of the headland of Park Head ({{gbmapping|SW840708}}) is a [[subvolcanic]] rock, [[dolerite]].

;Dark Sky discovery site
In 2014, the area was granted "Dark Sky" status by the [[Science and Technology Facilities Council]]. Dark Sky discovery sites must be free from light pollution and have good views of stars and the [[Milky Way]], and be accessible to the public.<ref>{{cite web|title=Cornwall gains two stargazing Dark Sky sites|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-cornwall-25681064|publisher=[[BBC]]|access-date=10 January 2014}}</ref>

'''Antony House''' is an early 18th-century property in the care of the [[National Trust]]. It is located between the town of [[Torpoint]] and the village of [[Antony, Cornwall|Antony]] in the county of [[Cornwall]], England, United Kingdom. It is a Grade I [[listed building]].

The house is faced in silvery-grey [[Pentewan stone]], flanked by colonnaded wings of mellow brick and overlooks the [[River Lynher]]. 

==History==
The house was built for [[Sir William Carew, 5th Baronet]] between 1718 and 1724, and ever since has continued as the primary residence of the Carew family, who have owned the estate since the mid-16th century. The [[Return of Owners of Land, 1873]] Survey recorded that the Carew-Pole Estates near [[Torpoint]] in Cornwall comprised 3,698 acres of land yielding an estimated £6,401.<ref name="OwnersOfLand1873_Cornwall_p5">“Return of Owners of Land, 1873 (County of Cornwall)”, House of Commons Sessional Papers, No. 1874 lixxii, p. 5. Retrieved 11 Nov 2025 from https://hdl.handle.net/2027/umn.31951d02468422h?urlappend=%3Bseq=177%3Bownerid=13510798899936106-191</ref>

[[Sir John Carew Pole, 12th Baronet]] gave the house and formal gardens into the care of the National Trust in 1961, on the understanding that the family could continue to reside there. Sir Tremayne Carew Pole, 14th Baronet, and his wife [[Charlotte Carew Pole|Charlotte]] currently live there with their two children. 

The house and gardens are open to the public between March and October.

==Collections and furnishings==

[[File:Thomas Coventry.jpg|thumb|One of the portraits held at Antony House: [[Thomas Coventry, 1st Baron Coventry]] by [[Cornelis Janssens van Ceulen]]]]

Antony House hosts a splendid collection of portraits, including a portrait of [[Charles I of England]] at his trial, (Charles I granted a baronetcy to the Poles in 1628). The collection contains some of Sir [[Joshua Reynolds]]' works, and a portrait of [[Ambrose Manaton (died 1696)|Rachel Carew]], believed to have inspired [[Daphne du Maurier]]'s novel ''[[My Cousin Rachel]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dumaurier.org/menu_page.php?id=108|title=Review of My Cousin Rachel|last=Willmore|first=Ann|year=2004|work=Daphne du Maurier website|access-date=21 August 2023}}</ref>

Rooms are heavily panelled in Dutch Oak and contain fine collections of 18th-century furnishings and textiles.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.plants.info/gardens/antony-house.htm |title=Antony House & Garden |accessdate=2009-07-18 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090401231202/http://www.plants.info/gardens/antony-house.htm |archivedate=2009-04-01 }}</ref>

==Gardens and estate==
The grounds were landscaped by [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] [[garden design]]er [[Humphry Repton]] and include the formal garden with the [[National Plant Collection|National Collection]] of [[Daylily|Day Lilies]].<ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-antony/  Anthony House] National Trust {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070911113412/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-antony/ |date=2007-09-11 }}</ref> In the early 19th century, yew hedges and [[topiary]] were added to the formal landscaping. Adorning the gardens are stone carvings from North West India, a Burmese temple bell brought to Antony by General Sir [[Reginald Pole-Carew (British Army officer)|Reginald Pole Carew]], statuary and more recently acquired modern [[sculpture]]s, including the Antony Cone water sculpture by [[William Pye (sculptor)|William Pye]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.williampye.com/sculpture-5.php?id%3D30 |title=William Pye - Antony Cone |accessdate=2009-09-29 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090424075716/http://www.williampye.com/sculpture-5.php?id=30 |archivedate=2009-04-24 }}</ref> This echoes the grand spectacle of the topiary yew cone nearby, which is almost as tall as the house itself. Other sculptures include ''Jupiter Stone'' by [[Peter Randall-Page]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://peterrandall-page.com/cv/wheretosee.htm |title=Peter Randall-Page, where to see his sculptures |accessdate=2009-05-25 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090402062813/http://peterrandall-page.com/cv/wheretosee.htm |archivedate=2009-04-02 }}</ref> and ''Hypercone'' by [[Simon Thomas (sculptor)|Simon Thomas]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://simonthomas-sculpture.com/gallery_larger.php |title=Gallery |publisher=Simon Thomas Sculpture |date= |accessdate=2018-10-29}}</ref>

Other notable features include a [[black walnut]] tree, [[Quercus suber|cork tree]], a Japanese ornamental pond and [[knot garden]]. The [[dovecote]] dates from the 18th century, while a [[folly]] has been added recently in the estate grounds.

=== Antony Woodland Garden ===
This informal [[woodland garden]] of {{Convert|60|acre|ha}} is owned by the Carew Pole Garden Trust and noted for its [[rhododendron]]s, [[azalea]]s, [[camellia]]s and [[magnolia]]s. It is recognised by the International Camelia Society as a "Garden of Excellence".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Antony Woodland Garden, Plymouth |url=https://internationalcamellia.org/en-us/europe-gardens-of-excellence/antony-woodland-garden-plymouth |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=internationalcamellia.org |language=en-us}}</ref> There are walks down to the [[River Lynher]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Us |url=https://antonywoodlandgarden.com/about/ |access-date=26 January 2024 |website=Antony Woodland Garden}}</ref> The Bath House situated in the Wilderness area of the garden is from the 18th century.<ref>{{Historic England|num=1159499|desc=Bath House|access-date=26 January 2024}}</ref>

==Film location==
Filming for the 2010 [[Disney]] film production of ''[[Alice in Wonderland (2010 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'', directed by [[Tim Burton]], took place in the grounds of Antony House in September 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gardensofcornwall.com/site/outdoor-kids/antony-house-and-garden-p133063 |title=Gardens in Cornwall |publisher=Gardensofcornwall.com |date= |accessdate=2018-10-29}}</ref> The estate was also used as a location for a [[Rosamunde Pilcher]] TV movie by German company [[ZDF]] with director [[Dieter Kehler]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0444936/|title=Dieter Kehler|publisher=IMDB|accessdate=29 October 2018}}</ref>
