23848973.title: East Pool mine
23848973.extract: East Pool mine (later known as East Pool and Agar mine), was a metalliferous mine in the Camborne and Redruth mining area, just east of the village of Pool in Cornwall. Worked from the early 18th century until 1945, first for copper and later tin, it was very profitable for much of its life. Today the site has two preserved beam engines and is part of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape World Heritage Site. It is owned by the National Trust.

main.*:
{{Short description|Former metalliferous mine in Cornwall, UK}} {{Use dmy dates|date=July 2023}} {{Use British English|date=February 2023}} {{Infobox mine | name = East Pool mine | image = Taylor's Shaft, East Pool MIne.jpg | width = | caption = The engine house and stack at Taylor's Shaft | pushpin_map = Cornwall | pushpin_label = East Pool mine | pushpin_map_caption = Location in Cornwall | coordinates = {{coord|50.2312|N|5.2622|W|region:GB|format=dms|display=inline,title}} | place = [[Redruth]] | subdivision_type = Unitary | state/province = [[Cornwall]] | country = UK | owner = [[National Trust]] | official website = [https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/east-pool-mine East Pool Mine] | acquisition year = | stock_exchange = | stock_code = | products = [[Copper]], [[tin]], [[arsenic]] and [[wolframite]] | financial year = | amount = | opening year = early 18th century | closing year = 1945 | embedded = {{Infobox historic site | embed = yes | designation1 = Scheduled monument | designation1_offname = East Pool Mine | designation1_date = 3 September 2004 | designation1_number = {{listed building England|1021323}} | designation2 = Grade II* | designation2_offname = Pump engine house at Taylor's Shaft of New East Pool Mine | designation2_date = 9 April 1975 | designation2_number = {{listed building England|1142600}} | designation3 = Grade II* | designation3_offname = Chimney stack approx. 30 metres east of pump engine house at Taylor's Shaft of New East Pool Mine | designation3_date = 9 April 1975 | designation3_number = {{listed building England|1328183}} | designation4 = Grade II | designation4_offname = East Pool Mine Engine House | designation4_date = 12 September 1989 | designation4_number = {{listed building England|1160518}} }} }} '''East Pool mine''' (later known as '''East Pool and Agar mine'''), was a [[Wikt:metalliferous|metalliferous]] mine in the [[Camborne]] and [[Redruth]] mining area, just east of the village of [[Pool, Cornwall|Pool]] in [[Cornwall]]. Worked from the early 18th century until 1945, first for copper and later tin, it was very profitable for much of its life. Today the site has two preserved [[beam engine]]s and is part of the [[Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape]] [[World Heritage Site]]. It is owned by the [[National Trust]]. ==Geology== The [[country rock (geology)|country rock]] at the mine is metamorphosed [[killas]] and [[Greenschist|greenstone]] overlying the [[Carn Brea, Redruth|Carn Brea]] granite. The many [[lode]]s on the [[Mining sett|sett]] are all crossed by several [[elvan]] [[Dike (geology)|dyke]]s. The mine's main produce was [[copper]] and later [[tin]], [[arsenic]] and [[wolframite]],Dines 1956, p. 326 also small amounts of the ores of [[bismuth]], [[cobalt]] and [[uranium]].Burt et al. 1987, pp. 383–389 ==History to 1900== East Pool mine started out in the early 18th century as a copper mine called "Pool Old Bal". The land under which it was allowed to mine (the "[[Mining sett|sett]]") was leased from the [[Basset family]] and it generated enough money for that family to build their country house at [[Tehidy Country Park|Tehidy]].{{Cite web |url = http://www.cornwallinfocus.co.uk/history/epal.php |title = East Pool and Agar Limited |publisher = Cornwall in Focus |access-date = 2009-08-03 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091104025711/http://www.cornwallinfocus.co.uk/history/epal.php |archive-date = 4 November 2009 }} The mine's [[adit]] was {{convert|32|fathom|ft m}} below ground and mining had taken place {{convert|16|fathom|ft m}} below this, the workings being drained by a [[flatrod]] system powered by a [[water wheel]] south of Pool village.Morrison 1980, p. 142 This phase of mining ceased in 1784. The mine restarted as East Pool mine in 1834. Its small sett (about 900 by 400 yards)Morrison 1980, p. 142 (map) was bounded on the west by [[South Crofty]] and [[Tincroft mine]]s, and on the south by the [[Carn Brea mine]]s. On its north was [[Wheal Agar]], with which it was later to merge. The mine had a very productive and long life, raising {{convert|91000|LT}} of copper ore and, later, {{convert|46000|LT}} of tin ore. In its early days the copper ore here was particularly rich, selling in 1835 for over £12 a long ton which was more than twice the average price at the time. This first profitable period lasted for ten years during which time a total of £32,256 dividends were paid on the 128 shares that had cost their owners a mere £5 each.Morrison 1980, p. 143 By 1843 the mine was employing 300 people and its deepest workings were at {{convert|90|fathom|ft m}}. However, a slump in the later 1840s almost caused the closure of the mine and its workings became partly flooded, which jeopardised the neighbouring South Crofty mine. This caused [[Frances Basset, 2nd Baroness Basset|Lady Basset]] to threaten to revoke the sett unless the mine was fully worked. The mine struggled on—one regular source of income was the monthly drainage charges totalling £60 that were paid by the neighbouring mines, including Wheal Agar—but it was not profitable again until 1854.Morrison 1980, pp. 143–145 In 1860 a rich body of ore containing [[wolframite]] was discovered. This ore has a similar [[specific gravity]] to [[cassiterite]] and the normal methods used for separating the ore from [[gangue]] could not separate these two minerals. To solve this problem a [[magnetic separation|Wetherill's Magnetic Separator]], which could process 10 tons of ore per day, was installed.Earl 1994, pp. 96–97 East Pool was one of the few mines, along with South Crofty, Tincroft, [[Dolcoath mine|Dolcoath]] and [[Wheal Basset]] and a few others, that were able to survive the depression of the [[Mining in Cornwall|Cornish mining industry]] in the late 19th century.{{Cite web |url = http://www.cornish-mining.org.uk/sites/camred.htm |title = Cornish Mining World Heritage – Camborne and Redruth Mining District |publisher = Cornwall Council |access-date = 2009-08-03 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090707015645/http://www.cornish-mining.org.uk/sites/camred.htm |archive-date = 7 July 2009 }} All these mines were close to one another and pumping water from the workings was still of highest priority: if any of the pumping engines stopped there were serious repercussions at the other mines. Such was the problem of underground water that their winding (whim) engines were adapted to haul water by using self-tipping water-skips—this was done at East Pool in 1897.Barton 1966, p. 78 East Pool mine still had a problem with water coming from Wheal Agar, which was losing money at the time and kept threatening to switch off its pumps, which it did in late 1895. The productive lower levels of East Pool flooded, meaning that it was restricted to reworking its older higher levels. Negotiations between the two mines continued for over a year until, after the intervention of [[Thomas Agar-Robartes, 6th Viscount Clifden|Lord Robartes]], who owned the Wheal Agar land, East Pool purchased Wheal Agar and all its equipment for £4,000, taking possession on 10 March 1897.Morrison 1980, pp. 158–159 ==After 1900== [[File:Trimming tin stone, East Pool Mine.jpg|thumb|left|A train hauled by a Camborne & Redruth tram locomotive]] Despite its problems, in almost every year from 1884 to 1913 more than 500 people were employed at the mine, with roughly half employed above ground and half underground. In 1913 the mine converted from a company that was run on the [[cost-book principle]] to a [[limited company]] called East Pool and Agar Ltd.{{Cite web |url=http://www.cornwall-calling.co.uk/mines/illogan/east-pool-agar.htm |title=East Pool Agar Mine, Cornwall |publisher=Cornwall Calling |access-date=2009-08-04 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090302170505/http://www.cornwall-calling.co.uk/mines/illogan/east-pool-agar.htm |archive-date=2 March 2009 }} Since the 1860s, the mine had had an extensive ore processing plant located just over a mile to the east in the [[Red River, Cornwall|Red River]] valley at Tolvaddon,Morrison 1980, pp. 145–146 and from 1903 until August 1934 ore was transported there via a mineral tramway which used part of the track of the [[Camborne and Redruth Tramways]], going through [[Pool, Cornwall|Pool village]].Trounson & Bullen 1999, pp. 102–103 After the tramway closed in 1934 the ore was carried by an [[aerial ropeway]] which ran directly across the countryside to the mill. This was a successful system that continued in use until the closure of the mine in 1945.Trounson & Bullen 1999, pp. 113–115 In 1921 there was a large rockfall underground which destroyed both of the mine's winding shafts,Trounson & Bullen 1999, p. 105 and caused flooding, so the next year a new [[Shaft mining|shaft]], named Taylor's Shaft after the mine manager, was started. In 1924 a notable {{convert|90|in|m|adj=on}} pumping engine was installed at this shaft, having been moved from [[Carn Brea mine]] where it had lain unused since 1914. It was known as ''Harvey's Engine'' and had been designed by [[Nicholas Trestrail]] and built in 1892 by [[Harvey & Co]]. It pumped water from the mine using seven lifts of pumps of {{convert|18|and|16|in|m|adj=on}} diameter.Barton 1966, pp. 242–243 The {{convert|110|ft|m|adj=mid|-tall}} chimney stack for this engine's boilers was completed before the engine house was built. The unique feature of this stack, the vertical letters "EPAL" displayed in white bricks near the top, is still visible. As well as standing for "East Pool and Agar Limited", "EPAL" was also the brand name of the arsenic sold by the company. The mine was taken over by its neighbour, [[South Crofty]], and closed in 1945, but Harvey's Engine continued to pump water out of the South Crofty workings until 28 September 1954, when it was replaced by electrical pumps. It is likely that the Harvey's engine would have been scrapped were it not for the intervention of a Mr Greville Bathe of [[Florida]], who purchased the engine and donated it to the [[Cornish Engines Preservation Committee]], who gave it to the National Trust in 1967.{{cite web |title=Cornish Engines |url=http://www.cornwall-online.co.uk/engine.htm |website=Cornwall Online |access-date=21 February 2019}} ==Today== Today, the site is within area A5 (The Camborne & Redruth Mining District){{Cite web |url = http://www.cornish-mining.org.uk/sites/camredlocationmap.htm |title = Cornish Mining World Heritage – Camborne-Redruth Mining District Location Map |publisher = Cornwall Council |access-date = 2009-08-03 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090709065950/http://www.cornish-mining.org.uk/sites/camredlocationmap.htm |archive-date = 9 July 2009 }} of the [[Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape]] [[World Heritage Site]], and two beam engines have been preserved here. Michell's Shaft Engine House ({{Coord| 50.2280|N| 5.2647|W|display=inline|type:landmark_region:GB}}) contains the last beam [[wikt:whim|whim]] engine to be installed in Cornwall. It has a cylinder of {{convert|30|in|m}} diameter and was built in 1887 by [[Holman Brothers]].Hancock 2008, pp. 89–91 It cost £675 and was designed to run at 27 strokes per minute and have a winding speed of {{convert|1000|ft/min|m/s}}.Barton 1966, p. 205 The engine was saved from being scrapped in 1941; it has been in the care of the National Trust since 1967 and since 1975 is still run on occasions.{{Cite web |url = http://www.cornish-mining.org.uk/sites/epal.htm |title = East Pool and Agar Mine |publisher = Cornwall Council |access-date = 2009-08-03 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081006105240/http://www.cornish-mining.org.uk/sites/epal.htm |archive-date = 6 October 2008 }} At Taylor's Shaft the [[National Trust]] has an Industrial Discovery Centre{{Cite web |url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-cornishminesandengines/ |title = Cornish Mines & Engines |publisher = National Trust |access-date = 2009-08-03 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090629061510/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-cornishminesandengines |archive-date = 29 June 2009 }} which incorporates several buildings dating from the 1920s. One of these is the engine house still containing the {{convert|90|in|m|adj=on}} Harvey's Engine, which was saved through a donation from an American benefactor.Barton 1966, p. 243 == Gallery == File:East Pool Mine Taylor's Shaft boilers.jpg|Taylor's shaft boilers File:East Pool Mine Taylors Shaft chimney.jpg|Taylor's shaft chimney File:East Pool Mine Taylor's Shaft loader lift cabins breaker and pumping engine house.jpg|Breaker in the background File:East Pool Mine Taylor's Shaft pump piston.jpg|Taylor's shaft pump house File:East Pool Mine Taylor's Shaft cage.jpg|Taylor's shaft cage File:East Pool mine, Michells Shaft engine house.jpg|The engine house at Michell's Shaft ==See also== {{Portal|Cornwall}} *[[Cornish steam engine]] *[[Mining in Cornwall and Devon]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Sources== {{Refbegin}} *{{Cite book | last=Barton | first=D. '''Cadson Bury''' is an [[British Iron Age|Iron Age]] [[hillfort]] about {{convert|2|mi|1}} south-west of [[Callington, Cornwall|Callington]], in [[Cornwall]], England.

It is owned by the [[National Trust]],<ref name=nt>[https://heritagerecords.nationaltrust.org.uk/HBSMR/MonRecord.aspx?uid=MNA100162 Cadsonbury Camp, Cadsonbury] National Trust Heritage Records Online. Retrieved 16 November 2017.</ref> and it is [[scheduled monument]].<ref name=historic>{{NHLE|num=1004494 |desc=Slight univallate hillfort called Cadson Bury|access-date= 16 November 2017}}</ref>

==Description==
The fort is sited in a commanding position on a steep hill, called Cadson Bury Down, above the [[River Lynher]].<ref name=historic/>

It is [[univallate]], probably of the early Iron Age.<ref name=wainwright>Richard Wainwright. ''A Guide to the Prehistoric Remains in Britain. Volume 1: South and East''. Constable, 1979. Page 42.</ref> The oval enclosure, longest from north to south, is about {{convert|275|m|0}} long and {{convert|170|m|0}} wide, enclosing an area of about {{convert|2.5|ha}}. The rampart is up to {{convert|2|m|0}} above the interior; the outer ditch is about {{convert|1.3|m|0}} deep on the east side, less visible elsewhere.<ref name=nt/><ref name=historic/>
[[File:Cadson Bury Digital Terrain Model.jpg|thumb|3D view of the digital terrain model]]
There are no traces of house platforms within the enclosure. There are two opposed inturned entrances on the east and west sides; the eastern entrance is clearly defined, the western entrance less so. Another entrance on the south may not be original.<ref name=nt/><ref name=historic/><ref name=book>''Cornwall's Archaeological Heritage''. The Historic Environment Unit, Cornwall County Council, 2003. Page 22.</ref>
